title: The Immortal Game
subtitle: Anderssen–Kieseritzky, London 1851 — two rooks and a queen, all given away.
goals: Value development and initiative above material
Finish with three minor pieces against a full army

steps.say: London, 1851 — a casual game between rounds that became the most famous game ever played. Anderssen has sacrificed a bishop, both rooks are hanging, and Black's queen is munching the queenside. Kieseritzky has grabbed everything on offer. Now count the pieces: White is about to be a queen and two rooks down, and he is completely winning — because every one of Black's pieces is still asleep at home.

steps.prompt: Both rooks hang and your queenside is gone. Play Anderssen's move — offer the second rook!
hints: Do not defend. Every tempo spent saving material lets Black develop and consolidate — the only currency here is TIME.
Bd6!! Ignore the rooks entirely: the bishop cuts the black king off from safety and prepares the mating net.

line.say: The immortal decision. The bishop is offered too, and it seals e7 — the square Black's king needs. Kieseritzky takes the rook on g1...
And still no defending! The pawn opens the f3 queen's diagonal toward the black king. Anderssen is now down a queen and two rooks and everything he owns is aimed at e8.
The king simply steps aside — because Black's captures have all been on the wrong side of the board. Three minor pieces now finish a game against a queen, two rooks and a bishop.

rejections.say: Saving the rook lets Black play ...Bb6 and ...Nc6 and consolidate an extra rook — the attack evaporates. The whole point of the Immortal Game: initiative expires, material doesn't. Spend the material.
A cheap check that achieves nothing after ...Kd8 — and worse, it removes a key attacker. Every move must build the mating net: Bd6 takes e7 away.

steps.wrongSay: Stop counting material. Which move takes the e7 escape square away from Black's king?
steps.successSay: Anderssen gave a bishop, two rooks and a queen — and every sacrifice bought a tempo.

steps.prompt: The finish. You are a queen and two rooks down — mate in three!
hints: Every remaining white piece touches the black king's box. Start with the check that drags him to the only square you can cover.
Nxg7+ Kd8, then the queen offers herself: Qf6+!! Nxf6 and the bishop mates on e7.

line.say: Check — the king must go to d8, into the net the d6 bishop built three moves ago...
THE queen sacrifice. It must be taken — and the capture drags Black's last defender away from e7...

CHECKMATE. Anderssen finishes with bishop, knight and knight — three minor pieces — while Black still owns a queen, two rooks and a bishop, nearly all of them on their starting squares. The most famous illustration in chess of a single idea: development and initiative are worth more than wood.

rejections.say: A check that lets the king slip to d8 while your attackers scatter — and Black's queen still guards the key squares. The correct order takes g7 FIRST, then offers the queen on f6.
Kd8! and the knight is simply lost with the attack. Every move of this finish must be forcing AND build the net: Nxg7+ is the only one that does both.

steps.wrongSay: Three white pieces, three moves, one mate. Begin with a check that forces the king to d8.
steps.successSay: 'The Immortal Game' — now played by you, sacrifices and all.
